### How do you estimate reliability using the Bayesian gamma prior model? {#sec-apr-46}

The [Bayesian paradigm](#sec-apr-1a) was introduced in Section 1 and Section 2 described the assumptions underlying the [gamma/exponential system model](#sec-apr-25) (including several methods to transform prior data and engineering judgment into gamma prior parameters "$a$" and "$b$"). Finally, we saw in Section 3 how to use this Bayesian system model to calculate the [required test time](#sec-apr-315) needed to confirm a system MTBF at a given confidence level.

[**Review of Bayesian procedure for the gamma exponential system model**]{#sec-apr-46-review}

The goal of Bayesian reliability procedures is to obtain as accurate a posterior distribution as possible, and then use this distribution to calculate failure rate (or MTBF) estimates with confidence intervals (called **credibility intervals** by Bayesians). @fig-apr-46-bayesum summarizes the steps in this process.

![Diagram illustrating the steps in Bayesian analysis](data-analysis/images/bayesian-update-summary.gif){#fig-apr-46-bayesum}

[**How to estimate the MTBF with bounds, based on the posterior distribution**]{#sec-apr-46-bounds}

Once the test has been run, and $r$ failures observed, the posterior gamma parameters are:

$$ a' = a + r, \,\,\,\,\, b' = b + T \, , $$

and a (median) estimate for the MTBF is calculated by

$$ \frac{1}{G^{-1}(0.5, \, a', \, 1/b')} \, , $$

where $G(q, \, \gamma, \, \beta)$ represents the gamma distribution with shape parameter $\gamma$, and scale parameter $\beta$. Some people prefer to use the reciprocal of the mean of the posterior distribution as their estimate for the MTBF. The mean is the **minimum mean square error** (MSE) estimator of $\lambda$, but using the reciprocal of the mean to estimate the MTBF is always more conservative than the "even money" 50% estimator.

A lower 80% bound for the MTBF is obtained from

$$ \frac{1}{G^{-1}(0.8, \, a', \, 1/b')} \, , $$

and, in general, a lower 100(1-$\alpha$)% lower bound is given by

$$ \frac{1}{G^{-1}(1-\alpha, \, a', \, 1/b')} \, . $$

A two-sided 100(1-$\alpha$/2)% credibility interval for the MTBF is

$$ \left[ \frac{1}{G^{-1}(1-\alpha/2, \, a', \, 1/b')} , \,\,\, \frac{1}{G^{-1}(\alpha/2, \, a', \, 1/b')} \right] \, . $$

Finally, the $G(1/M, \, a', \, 1/b')$ calculates the probability that MTBF is greater than $M$.

**Example**

[**A Bayesian example to estimate the MTBF and calculate upper and lower bounds**]{#sec-apr-46-example}

A system has completed a reliability test aimed at confirming a 600 hour MTBF at an 80% confidence level. Before the test, a gamma prior with $a$ = 2, $b$ = 1400 was agreed upon, based on testing at the vendor's location. Bayesian test planning calculations, allowing up to 2 new failures, called for a test of 1909 hours. When that test was run, there actually were exactly two failures. What can be said about the system?

The posterior gamma CDF has parameters $a'$ = 4 and $b'$ = 3309. The plot below shows CDF values on the $y$-axis, plotted against $1/\lambda$ = MTBF, on the $x$-axis. By going from probability, on the $y$-axis, across to the curve and down to the MTBF, we can estimate any MTBF percentile point.

```{r}
#| label: fig-apr-46-posterior-cdf
#| fig-cap: "Plot of posterior (after test) gamma distribution"
#| code-fold: true
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)

a_prime <- 4
b_prime <- 3309

mtbf_seq <- seq(100, 3000, length.out = 300)
cdf_seq <- pgamma(1 / mtbf_seq, shape = a_prime, rate = b_prime)

ggplot(tibble(mtbf = mtbf_seq, cdf = cdf_seq), aes(mtbf, cdf)) +
  geom_line(color = "blue") +
  labs(x = "MTBF (hours)", y = "CDF") +
  theme_classic()
```

The MTBF values are shown below.

```{r}
#| label: verify-apr-46-mtbf-percentiles
#| code-fold: true
percentiles <- c(0.9, 0.8, 0.5, 0.1)
mtbf_values <- 1 / qgamma(percentiles, shape = a_prime, rate = b_prime)

tibble(
  Expression = c(
    "1/G^-1(0.9, 4, 1/3309)",
    "1/G^-1(0.8, 4, 1/3309)",
    "1/G^-1(0.5, 4, 1/3309)",
    "1/G^-1(0.1, 4, 1/3309)"
  ),
  `MTBF (hours)` = round(mtbf_values)
) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lr")
```

The R computation above matches NIST's reported MTBF percentiles (495, 600, 901, and 1897 hours) exactly.

The test has confirmed a 600 hour MTBF at 80% confidence, a 495 hour MTBF at 90% confidence and (495, 1897) is a 90% credibility interval for the MTBF. A single number (point) estimate for the system MTBF would be 901 hours. Alternatively, you might want to use the reciprocal of the mean of the posterior distribution $(b'/a')$ = 3309/4 = 827 hours as a single estimate. The reciprocal mean is more conservative, in this case it is a 57% lower bound $(G(4/3309, \, 4, \, 1/3309))$.

```{r}
#| label: verify-apr-46-reciprocal-mean
#| code-fold: true
recip_mean <- b_prime / a_prime
confidence_level <- pgamma(a_prime / b_prime, shape = a_prime, rate = b_prime)

tibble(Statistic = c("Reciprocal mean MTBF", "Confidence level"), Value = c(round(recip_mean), paste0(round(confidence_level * 100), "%"))) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lr")
```

The R computation above matches NIST's reported reciprocal mean (827 hours) and confidence level (57%) exactly.

The analyses in this section can be implemented using R code.
